analysis.one_liner: Bars states that take Medicaid money from banning IVF fertility treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicaid law so that any state receiving federal Medicaid money cannot ban in vitro fertilization, and cannot let its local governments ban it either. It does not require anyone to provide IVF and does not stop states from setting health and safety rules for the procedure. It was introduced late in the 118th Congress and never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, couples who need IVF to have children would gain a federal guarantee that no state taking Medicaid money — which is every state — can ban the procedure, and no local government within those states can ban it either. Fertility clinics would gain legal certainty that IVF remains lawful wherever Medicaid operates.

how_it_helps.text: It amends Medicaid law so that any state wanting federal Medicaid money cannot ban IVF, and cannot allow its local governments to ban it either.
It expressly does not force any individual or organization to provide IVF services, and does not stop states from setting health and safety rules for the practice.

analysis.who_pays: States would give up the power to ban IVF if they want to keep receiving federal Medicaid funds; no one bears a direct financial cost, since the bill does not fund IVF itself.

drawbacks.text: The bill only forbids state bans on IVF; it does not require insurance coverage of IVF, make Medicaid itself pay for IVF services, or lower its cost, so it would not make IVF affordable for most families.

It ties federal Medicaid funds to a condition on state law, a lever critics of federal Medicaid conditions generally object to, and its narrow carve-outs could be litigated over how far state health-and-safety rules may go.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow but low-cost: it does not fund IVF or expand coverage, so its practical benefit would be limited to states that might otherwise ban the practice. The main drawback is that it does little to address the actual barriers families face — IVF typically costs $10,000-$20,000 or more per cycle with limited insurance coverage — and its shield against future state bans has never been tested. Its chief cost is political: restricting what states may do on abortion-adjacent policy draws constitutional objections, and the bill was never seriously pursued.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever acted on it before the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on June 27, 2024, with Rep. Nancy Mace as the other original cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost directly, since the bill never advanced; the legal landscape for IVF stays exactly as it was, with any future state ban decision left to the states.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the legal status quo held

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its Medicaid condition barring state IVF bans.

for.name: Rep. Nancy Mace
for.what_they_did: Joined as the other original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Republicans, but with only two cosponsors and no votes on record there is no way to tell how the parties would have split.

industries.note: By barring states from prohibiting IVF as a condition of Medicaid funding, the bill protects the legal foundation of the fertility industry nationwide. It does not expand coverage or payment, so clinics gain legal certainty rather than new revenue. Its interest runs alongside the public's here, since families need clinics to keep operating.

States would lose the ability to prohibit IVF while keeping authority to regulate its safety, all under the financial leverage of federal Medicaid payments. This mainly affects any state considering a future ban rather than current practice.
